lessons.title: State Representation: What Should the Agent Actually See?

body.text: More features are not automatically a better state. Every feature added multiplies the space of situations the agent has to learn about, and a real market never hands the agent everything relevant anyway. Good state design is about building the smallest, most honest summary that still captures what matters.

children.text: From a Feature List to a State Vector: What Changed Since Chapter 1

Chapter 1 built a six-feature state vector: momentum, RSI, volume anomaly, India VIX, position, and unrealized P&L. It is tempting to keep adding more, order book imbalance, sector momentum, a dozen technical indicators, on the theory that more information can only help. It cannot, past a point, and the reason has a name: the curse of dimensionality.
The Curse of Dimensionality: Why More Features Isn't Automatically Better

Every additional feature multiplies the size of the space of possible states the agent might encounter, and an agent needs to see a given state, or something close enough to it, many times before it can estimate its value reliably. A simplified illustration using binary features makes the growth rate concrete.

stats.label: 5 Binary Features
stats.context: 2^5, small enough for an agent to see each state repeatedly

stats.label: 10 Binary Features
stats.context: 2^10, already thinning out how often any one state repeats

stats.label: 20 Binary Features
stats.context: 2^20, most states now seen rarely or never during training

children.text: Real trading features are continuous, not binary, so the actual explosion is worse than this illustration, not better; the intuition still holds exactly. Every feature added to a state vector needs to earn its place by capturing something genuinely predictive that the existing features do not already capture, not simply by being available.
Lookback Windows: Giving the Agent Memory Without Breaking the Markov Property

A more disciplined way to give an agent a sense of recent history, instead of hand-picking an ever-longer list of derived indicators, is to stack a short window of recent raw or lightly processed observations directly into the state. A state built from the last 10 minutes of returns and volume, rather than a single handful of summary statistics, lets the agent's own learned function discover whatever pattern in that window matters, instead of a human deciding in advance that RSI and a 5-day return are the only patterns worth encoding.

body.code:
import numpy as np

def build_state(prices, volumes, position, unrealized_pnl, window=10):
    returns = np.diff(prices[-(window + 1):]) / prices[-(window + 1):-1]
    recent_volumes = np.array(volumes[-window:])
    volume_z = (recent_volumes - recent_volumes.mean()) / (recent_volumes.std() + 1e-8)
    state = np.concatenate([
        returns,            # last `window` step returns
        volume_z,           # last `window` step volume, z-scored within this window
        [position, unrealized_pnl],
    ])
    return state
body.caption: A 10-step lookback window turns the last 10 minutes into part of the state itself, rather than compressing it into a single indicator. The state size grows with the window length, so this is the same curse-of-dimensionality tradeoff as before, traded off deliberately rather than accidentally.

children.text: Window length is itself a hyperparameter with the same tradeoff as the feature count above: too short, and the agent misses patterns that unfold over more steps than the window covers; too long, and the state grows large enough to reintroduce the exact sparsity problem lookback windows were meant to avoid, on top of slowing down training and inference.
Partial Observability: When the Market Knows More Than the Agent Does

markDefs.definition: Partially Observable Markov Decision Process: an MDP where the agent does not observe the true underlying state directly, only an observation that gives incomplete or noisy information about it. The agent has to act based on a belief about the true state, built from its observation history, rather than the true state itself.

children.text: There is a deeper honesty worth having about all of this. Chapter 2's Markov Decision Process formalism assumes the agent's state fully captures everything relevant to the future. No feature vector built from public price, volume, and volatility data actually achieves this for a real market. Other participants hold information, institutional order flow not yet visible, macro views not yet priced in, faster data from colocated infrastructure, that a retail-accessible feature set simply cannot see. Formally, this makes real trading closer to a

This is not a reason to abandon the MDP framework, every algorithm in this course still applies, it is a reason to see state design differently: a good state vector is not a claim that it captures the true state of the market. It is an attempt to build a sufficient statistic, a compressed summary of everything observable that is useful for predicting what matters next, standing in for a true state the agent will never fully see.
Normalization and Scaling: Keeping Features Comparable and Stationary

Whatever features make up the state, they need to be normalized so the agent can compare and combine them sensibly, and this is exactly where Chapter 1's look-ahead bias warning applies most directly. Normalizing using statistics computed over the entire dataset, including data the agent would not have had access to at the time, leaks future information into training. The correct approach normalizes using only a trailing window of past data at each point in time, computed the same way live as it was in training.

cells: Mean and standard deviation computed once, over the entire dataset, including future data
Look-ahead bias; performs unrealistically well in backtest, degrades live
Mean and standard deviation computed only from a trailing window ending at the current step
Correct approach; matches what would actually be available live, at the cost of noisier early-window estimates
Uses log(price_t / price_t-1) instead of raw price or simple percentage return
Naturally more stationary and additive across time; a common first transformation before any further normalization

children.text: Rolling normalization costs something: early in a window, the mean and standard deviation estimates are noisier, and the agent has to learn to be appropriately less confident when normalization statistics are still settling in. That cost is the price of a state design that behaves identically in backtesting and in live deployment, which is the entire point.

body.title: Choosing a Lookback Window Length
body.scenario: Two researchers disagree about lookback window length for an intraday Nifty 50 agent. One wants a 3-minute window, arguing it keeps the state small and training fast. The other wants a 60-minute window, arguing it captures more of the session's structure.
body.prompt: What tradeoff is each researcher underweighting, and how would you approach choosing between them?
body.modelAnswer: The 3-minute researcher is underweighting the risk of missing patterns that genuinely unfold over a longer horizon, a slow-building momentum shift or a volatility regime change within the session simply will not be visible in a 3-minute window, no matter how well the agent learns from what little it can see. The 60-minute researcher is underweighting the curse of dimensionality and training cost: a much larger state space means the agent needs proportionally more training data to see comparable states repeatedly, and training and inference both become slower. Rather than picking one length by argument, the more disciplined approach is to treat window length as a hyperparameter, train and validate candidate windows, perhaps 5, 15, 30, and 60 minutes, on a common training period, and compare their out-of-sample performance rather than trusting either researcher's intuition alone.

body.title: Why the Full-Dataset Normalization Approach Is Wrong
body.question: A dataset spans 2019 to 2024. A researcher computes the mean and standard deviation of a feature across the entire 2019 to 2024 dataset, then uses those fixed values to normalize the feature for every day in the dataset, including days from 2019. What is the core problem with this approach?
options: There is no problem; using the full dataset produces the most statistically precise mean and standard deviation

It introduces look-ahead bias, since the normalization statistics used for a 2019 data point were computed using information from 2020 through 2024 that would not actually have been available at the time
It only matters for options data, not futures or equity data
The problem is computational speed, not statistical validity
body.explanation: Using the full dataset's mean and standard deviation to normalize a 2019 data point means that data point's normalized feature value depends on price behavior from years after it that would not have existed yet at the time. This is a textbook case of look-ahead bias, the same category of error Chapter 1 warned about, here appearing specifically in the mechanics of state feature normalization. The fix is a rolling, trailing-window normalization that only ever uses data available up to that point in time.

points: Adding more features to a state vector is not automatically better; the curse of dimensionality means each added feature multiplies the size of the state space, thinning out how often the agent sees any specific state repeated during training

Stacking a short lookback window of recent raw observations gives an agent access to recent history directly, letting its own learned function discover relevant patterns instead of a human hand-picking indicators, at the cost of the same dimensionality tradeoff
Real trading is better modeled as a POMDP than a true MDP, since no feature set built from public data captures everything relevant that other, better-informed participants can see
A good state design is best understood as an attempt to build a sufficient statistic, a useful compressed summary of what's observable, not a claim to capture the market's true underlying state
State features must be normalized using only a rolling, trailing window of past data, never statistics computed over the full dataset, or normalization itself becomes a source of look-ahead bias
Window length, like every other design choice in this chapter, is a hyperparameter to validate empirically across candidate values, not a decision to make by intuition alone
